articles.title: Four domains and one wrong type: the 54 minutes Control D's paid DNS went dark
articles.excerpt: On a Sunday afternoon in October, paying customers of Control D lost the internet. Not some of it. All of it, on every device, in every location, for about 54 minutes. Their phones showed no connectio…
articles.body: On a Sunday afternoon in October, paying customers of Control D lost the internet. Not some of it. All of it, on every device, in every location, for about 54 minutes. Their phones showed no connection. Their laptops showed no connection. Even phones on mobile data, using a persistent Control D profile, looked dead. To most of the people affected, it felt like the internet itself had gone down. It had not. The free service kept working the whole time. No query was answered wrongly, and no customer data was touched. What stopped was much smaller and much stranger: four domain names, saved with one wrong data type, in a configuration file that every paid DNS server read at the same moment. This is a story about a type mismatch.
articles.author: Kashif Manzer

articles.title: Fanning out map markers in screen pixels, not map units
articles.excerpt: I make Last Thaw, a free browser strategy game. Up to a hundred players start with five settlers on a real map of Earth, cut into 408 regions, and have 30 real days to build an empire while an ice age…
articles.body: I make Last Thaw , a free browser strategy game. Up to a hundred players start with five settlers on a real map of Earth, cut into 408 regions, and have 30 real days to build an empire while an ice age advances from both poles. It's in early access and I'm looking for people to test it. Everything that moves in the game is drawn on that map: settlers heading for a new region, caravans hauling goods, armies on the way to a raid, canoes and later ships on the sea lanes. Each one is a small round marker sitting on its route. This post is about one small bug in those markers that taught me something I should have known going in: some things on a zoomable map belong to the world, and some belong to the screen. Mixing them up gave me caravans swimming in the ocean. The setup The map is one SVG.

articles.title: How we built an AI that fixes failed builds (and why we verify the patch before building)
articles.excerpt: It's Tuesday, 11 p.m. The demo is at nine. You push one last change to your We run a hosting platform for AI agents, and that moment is the one we wanted Fix . One click, and a fixed copy of your agen…
articles.body: It's Tuesday, 11 p.m. The demo is at nine. You push one last change to your agent, and the deploy fails: a dependency you installed locally and never wrote down, a variable you renamed in one file and not the other, a port your framework picked by itself. The error is somewhere in three hundred lines of build log. We run a hosting platform for AI agents, and that moment is the one we wanted to remove. Not with a chatbot that explains the log, but with a button: Fix with AI . One click, and a fixed copy of your agent is live a few minutes later, or you are told clearly why not. The hard part turned out not to be "ask a model for a patch". It was everything around the model. This is how it works, and what each part taught us. Triage first: is this even a code problem?

articles.title: We let an AI red-team our hardware encryption. Here's what it found.
articles.excerpt: I build Crypt-in alone, in Bologna. It's file encryption anchored to a €5 ESP32-S3: the root secret is generated on the chip at first boot and no command in the protocol exports it. Files open while t…
articles.body: I build Crypt-in alone, in Bologna. It's file encryption anchored to a €5 ESP32-S3: the root secret is generated on the chip at first boot and no command in the protocol exports it. Files open while the dongle is plugged in. Pull it out and the session closes in under five seconds. A product like that has an obvious problem. Its author is the worst person to judge it. So in August I handed it to an AI and asked it to break it. This post is what came back, including the two places where our own conclusions turned out to be wrong. One thing up front, because it shapes everything below: this was me running sessions with an AI. It is not an independent audit , and the report says so. That's exactly why the second half of this post is an invitation.
articles.author: Tommy

articles.title: Design Instagram's feed: system design in 5 steps
articles.excerpt: A home feed must return the newest posts from every account a user follows, in time order, within a latency budget, while reads outnumber posts by about a hundred to one. The design question is where…
articles.body: A home feed must return the newest posts from every account a user follows, in time order, within a latency budget, while reads outnumber posts by about a hundred to one. The design question is where the work of merging those posts happens: on every read, on every write, or split between the two, and what each choice costs in operations, memory and tail latency. Interview question: "Design the home feed of a photo app for 100 million daily users." Prerequisites Requests per second and peak load. Capacity is planned for the busiest second: divide a daily count by 86,400, then multiply by a stated peak factor, as in the ticket sale spike that separates performance from scalability . Big-O cost. O(log N) means the work grows with the logarithm of the input size: doubling N adds one step.

articles.body: I'm a photographer. Well, more of a hobbyist, but still. However, my main interest in broad computer science invades my photographic choices heavily. From very early on I used webp, as an alternative to JPEG, then I jumped to AVIF when it became widely supported. It beats JPEG on quality per byte by a wide margin. The problem is: AVIF encoders suck. Well, they were never designed for still images, after all AVIF is a byproduct of the video world. Most AVIF encoders are slow, weirdly tuned out of the box for images, and not ergonomic at all. This is the story of avif-converter , the tool that came out of it. articles.body: Thanks to a combination of radar, infrasound, dash-cam and security camera footage, astronomers have tracked the bright daytime meteor that fell over Cape Cod Bay in May 2026 back to its origin as a small asteroid perturbed by Jupiter and sent on a comet-like orbit towards Earth. Meteor fireballs visible in the daytime are referred to as 'bolides'. At 1:06 p.m. local time (18:06 UTC) on May 30, 2026 one such bolide was widely witnessed falling out of the sky over coastal Massachusetts, with members of the public also reporting an associated sonic boom that rumbled across the north-eastern coast of the United States.

articles.body: CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA is pushing ahead with its plan to build a moon base for astronauts by 2032, with the agency unveiling up to $10 billion in contracts to launch and deliver cargo to the moon and other efforts on Saturday (Nov. 7). The NASA announcement, revealed here during the space agency's "Max Power" air show event at Kennedy Space Center , included plans for a new $10 billion Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) framework, dubbed CLPS 2, about$1.3 billion in funding for the agency's Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) program, and the nuclear-powered "PROMISE" rover on the moon.

articles.excerpt: "I promise you, there'll be more to come."
articles.body: CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman knows how to make an entrance. Under the bright afternoon sun on Saturday (Nov. 7), Isaacman plummeted through the air above 10,000 onlookers, skydiving into the agency's air show MAX POWER. MAX POWER overtook NASA's Kennedy Space Center here over the weekend, combining aeronautics and aerospace in a massive public air show, the first of its kind for the space agency. A mix of astronauts, fighter jet displays and new technology on display, the spectacle is a lot space-ier than a traditional air show, and Isaacman made sure to really showcase this merging of worlds.

articles.body: A satellite went knee-deep in the dead, after a voice command from the ground activated the Doom video game in space. Playing a first-person shooter from 1993 was obviously not in the design plan for the PRETTY cubesat , which is run by a consortium including the European Space Agency (ESA). But the pioneering voice command opens up new worlds for satellite work, the team says. "Someone in distress at sea or in a remote area could transmit 'mayday' or "help" on a radio," stated Estonia's Tanagra Space, which supplied the software for the feat. The hope is one day, a satellite could use transcription and AI to alert rescue services for assisting folks in remote zones. The call to play Doom, thankfully, had no other urgency than curiosity — and teamwork, fueled by pizza.

articles.title: The climate case for AI has not been made
articles.excerpt: This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence. The host has already called on coun…
articles.body: This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action. But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet, despite some very optimistic claims from AI companies.
